title: Inside Day
teaches: The inside day as we trade it: a quiet bar whose high and low both sit inside the prior day's, used as an entry tool inside a bigger setup in a leader above its 200-day, bought as price trades over the high, with the stop a few cents under the inside day's low, the buy off if the low trades first, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail, and the knowledge that the bar alone is near random while the stock, the location and the market carry the edge.

walkthroughs.title: NVDA, January 2024: four days after the breakout
steps: NVDA broke out in January 2024. Four days later, an inside day on light volume, above a rising 50 and 200-day.
Small and quiet, 36% of the mother bar. A tad extended from the 50, but it's a leader resting after a breakout.
January 16 it opens 0.1% over the trigger. Buy at market, 55.02. Stop a few cents under the inside low, 54.28.
If the break fails and the stop goes, we're wrong. Instead 3R came in two days. The first sell is your call.

walkthroughs.title: MPC, January 2013: a quiet day after a shelf
steps: MPC, January 2013. A two-week shelf on its rising short-term averages, then an inside day closing near its high.
Volume's light, 0.66x the mother bar. Quiet, and in a good spot. The spot carries this trade, not the bar.
January 15 it trades through the high. Buy at market, 31.33. Stop a few cents under the low, 30.90: 1.37% risk.
If the low trades first, we're wrong. Instead 3R came the next day. We still rarely sell on day one.

walkthroughs.title: VST, December 2023: the slow one and the trail
steps: Not every winner is fast. VST, December 2023: a plain inside day in a slow, orderly trend.
December 22 it trades over the high. Buy at market, 38.00. Stop a few cents under the inside day's low, 37.53.
Then it crawls. A stall under 1R after 10 days gets sold. This one just made it: 3R right on day 10.
Sell some into a push, trail the rest. It ran to 60R. In our testing, buys with no trail lose on average.

questions.q: The last bar on this chart looks quiet. What has to be true before you call it an inside day?
choices: High and low both inside yesterday's
Narrowest range of the last seven days
questions.answer: High and low both inside yesterday's
questions.why: High and low, both inside yesterday's. That's the whole test. On FTNT's last bar the high stays under yesterday's high and the low stays above yesterday's low. The open and the close don't decide it. Neither does how narrow it is, because a narrow day can still poke out the top. When the whole day fits inside the day before, buyers and sellers took a breather. That gives you a clean level to buy over and a clean low to risk against.
questions.lesson_line: Both ends inside yesterday's bar. That's the whole definition.

wrong.It closed inside yesterday's range: The close is one print. You check the high and the low of the whole day.
wrong.Narrowest range of the last seven days: That's an NR7. A narrow day can still poke over yesterday's high, and then it isn't inside.
wrong.It opened inside yesterday's range: The open is one price. A day can open inside and still run out the top later.

questions.simple: Both ends have to sit inside yesterday's bar. The open, the close and how narrow it is don't decide it.

reasons: five sources agree; the key uses only the part that strict and tie rules share

questions.story: The last bar on the chart is today.

deeper.counter: Crabel, Bulkowski, Mish and TraderLion all define it the same way: the whole day inside the prior day. Crabel and Bulkowski want a strictly lower high and higher low. Brooks allows a tie. None of these questions hang on one.

questions.q: A clean inside day is a reason to buy a stock on its own, wherever the stock sits.
questions.why: False. The inside day is how we get in, not why we're in. On its own the bar is close to random. When we tested every inside day, only about one in four reached 3R. What makes it work is the stock, where it sits, and the market. Think of a leader just after a breakout, resting at a rising 20 EMA, in a Green market. Then the quiet day hands you a tight trigger and a stop right under it.
questions.lesson_line: The inside day is how you get in. The setup is what you're getting into.
questions.simple: False. The bar is just the way in, and the stock, the spot and the market are why it works.

reasons: one source: the criteria card, a proposed criterion

questions.q: You plan to buy over this inside day's high tomorrow. Where does your stop go?
choices: A few cents under the inside day's low
A few cents under the mother bar's low
A few cents under your entry price
Seven percent under your fill price
questions.answer: A few cents under the inside day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the inside day's low. That low is the low of the day (LOD) for the quiet bar, and it's where the idea is wrong. If price trades back under it, the pause failed. For MPC that put the stop at 30.90 against a 31.33 buy, 1.37% away. That's a small loss if it fails, which is the whole appeal of this bar. A few cents under, not right on it, so one tick doesn't take you out.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first. A few cents under the inside day's low.

wrong.A few cents under the mother bar's low: That's the mistake. It widens the stop for comfort, and then you size it like it's still tight.
wrong.A few cents under your entry price: That's no room at all. Normal wiggle takes you out before the trade can work.
wrong.Seven percent under your fill price: That's way past where the chart says you're wrong. We like 1 to 3%, and 5% is the most we'll take.

questions.simple: Just under the inside day's low. That's where the pause fails, and it keeps the loss small.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, F62)
fixed before

questions.story: The last bar is the inside day. The buy is over its high tomorrow.

deeper.counter: Bulkowski's tip is to close out at a 7% loss against the breakout. That's his rule, not ours. Kullamagi puts the stop at the low of the day, which is where ours goes too.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: An inside-day buy needs the close above the ___-day, with the 50-day above it.
questions.why: 200. The inside-day card needs the close above the 200-day, with the 50-day above the 200-day. That keeps us out of longs below the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200, the 50 over the 200. Then look at the bar.
questions.simple: It is the 200-day, because we buy no longs below that line.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: The bigger bar right before an inside day, the one it fits inside, is called the mother bar.
questions.why: True. The mother bar is the bigger day right before, the one the quiet day fits inside. You need the name because it has its own levels. The inside day's high is your trigger and its low is your stop. The mother bar's high and low sit outside that, the wider frame. Don't hang your stop on the mother low just to give it room. That widens your risk for comfort.
questions.lesson_line: Two bars. The mother bar, and the quiet day inside it.
questions.simple: True. It's the bigger day the quiet day fits inside, and your levels come from the quiet day.

reasons: a naming convention from the card, not a word the web sources use

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A double inside day is ___ inside days in a row, each inside the day before.
questions.why: Two. A double inside day is two inside days in a row, each inside the day before. A triple is three. Mish says two in a row is an even clearer sign of indecision.
questions.lesson_line: Two quiet days, each inside the last. The spring winds tighter.
questions.simple: Two. A double inside day is two quiet days in a row, each one inside the day before.

reasons: the card's alternate reading of a double also gives two

questions.q: Volume lighter than the mother bar is preferred on an inside day, not required.
questions.why: True. Lighter than the mother bar is preferred, not required. TraderLion: best when the inside bar comes on low volume; Morpheus wants it on lighter volume too.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet volume on the quiet day is a plus, not a must.

questions.q: In our test, inside-day buys with a fixed stop and no sells into strength lost money on average. What fixes that?
questions.why: Trail the winners. In our test most buys got stopped, 88.2% of them inside 60 days. The few that ran have to pay for all of those. A fixed stop with no plan to ride them hands the runners back. So we sell some into a 3, 5 or 7 day push and trail the rest on the 9 or 20 EMA. That keeps you in the big ones. To be fair, the test never tried sells and a trail. It only showed the bar needs them.
questions.lesson_line: Most of these get stopped. Ride the ones that work.

wrong.Use a wider stop: A wider stop just means fewer shares for the same risk. It does nothing for the winners.
wrong.Buy only the tiniest bars: Tinier isn't better. A sliver's low sits right in the day's noise.
wrong.Size up on every buy: Bigger size makes every loss bigger too. Size comes from the stop, not from hope.

questions.simple: Trail the winners. Most buys get stopped, so the few runners have to be ridden.

deeper.trap: Don't read this as proof that a trail wins. The scan used a fixed stop and no sells, so it never tested one. It shows the bar alone isn't an edge, and that the winners carry the whole thing.

reasons: a number from our own test that can be rerun (88.2%)
fixed before

questions.q: The inside day's high is 50.00. Tomorrow it gaps up over it. What's the highest open you'd still buy?
questions.why: 52.00. We'll buy a gap over the trigger at the open if it's no more than 4% over the inside day's high. 50.00 plus 4% is 52.00. Above that it isn't this setup anymore. Your stop is still down under the inside day's low, so a bigger gap stretches the risk and shrinks your shares. Do the math the night before, so you're not doing it in the first minute.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent over the high is the line. Know it before the open.
questions.simple: Up to 4% over the high, so 52.00. Past that it's a gap trade, not this setup.

reasons: a computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)
fixed before

wrong.$48.00: That's 4% under the high. The line sits above it.
wrong.$50.20: The decimal slipped. 4% of 50.00 is two dollars, not twenty cents.

questions.q: Two sessions before earnings, a clean inside day prints. You can still buy the break tomorrow.
questions.why: False. We don't open new buys in the 3 days before a report, and tomorrow is inside that window. The problem is the gap. Earnings can open the stock way under your stop, and no stop order catches that. A tight inside-day stop doesn't save you there. Let the report pass, then look again. We only hold through one when we're already up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Stay three days clear of a report. You can't stop a gap.
questions.simple: False. No new buys in the 3 days before earnings, because a report can gap right through your stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: It broke the inside day's low before it ever touched the high. What happens to your buy?
choices: It's off, the low went first
Nothing, keep waiting for the high
Buy here, it's a better price
Wait to see if it closes under
questions.answer: It's off, the low went first
questions.why: It's off. Which side trades first matters. The low going first tells you the pause failed and sellers won the first round. Cancel the order over the high. If it later climbs back through the high, that's a stock that just shook people out, and it needs a fresh look. Buying down here isn't a better price. You'd be buying right where your stop was supposed to be.
questions.lesson_line: Whichever side goes first decides it. Low first, the buy is off.

wrong.Nothing, keep waiting for the high: That plan died when the low traded. A break of the high now comes after a failed pause.
wrong.Buy here, it's a better price: You'd be buying under the level that was your stop. That's not this trade.
wrong.Wait to see if it closes under: You don't wait for the close. The low trading first is enough to call off the buy.

questions.story: Your buy is set for a trade over the inside day's high. The stock opens flat and trades under the inside day's low at 9:45.
questions.simple: The buy is off. The low broke first, so the pause failed.

reasons: one source: the criteria card, a proposed criterion

questions.q: We take inside days in leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group.
questions.why: True. Buy leaders: an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet bar in a laggard is still a laggard. Buy the leaders.

questions.q: One inside day is a sliver with the stop just 0.8% away. Another is a normal pause. Is the sliver better?
questions.why: No. A sliver looks great because the stop is tiny. But a stop 0.8% away sits right in the stock's normal daily wiggle. One ordinary dip and you're out before the trade had a chance. A normal pause with its low at a real level gives the stop something to stand on. How narrow the bar is doesn't make the setup better. The stock and where it sits do.
questions.lesson_line: A sliver isn't a tight stop. Its low sits in the noise.

wrong.Yes, tighter means stronger: Narrow just means quiet. It doesn't mean the next move is bigger.
wrong.Yes, the stop is smaller: The stop sets your share count. One that small sits inside normal noise and gets hit.
wrong.Same, only the shape counts: How wide the bar is matters for the stop. A sliver's low is in the noise.

questions.simple: No. The sliver's stop sits inside normal noise, so it gets hit for no reason.

deeper.counter: An NR4 is the narrowest range in four days, an NR7 the narrowest in seven (StockCharts). That says the day was quiet. It doesn't say it's better.

reasons: one source for the key: the criteria card, a cue
fixed before

questions.q: Clean bar, great stock, Red market. What's the play?
choices: Buy it, a leader is a leader
Buy it at half the size
questions.why: Pass. Red is the weakest reading on our market filter, and in Red we're mostly in cash. The reading is a guide, not a law. But breakouts fail a lot more when the market isn't behind them. The stock and the bar can be perfect and still get dragged down with everything else. Keep it on your radar. When the market turns, the names that held up in Red are the ones I want first.
questions.lesson_line: The best bar in a Red market is still just a bar. Sit on your hands.

wrong.Buy it, a leader is a leader: The stock is one part of the edge. The market is another, and right now it says wait.
wrong.Buy it at half the size: Smaller size on a trade the market's fighting is still a trade the market's fighting.
wrong.Short it, Red favors shorts: Shorts are for weak stocks breaking down. This leader is holding up. Red cuts the buying, it doesn't make a leader a short.

questions.story: The market filter in our app reads Red. A leader above its 200-day prints a clean inside day after a breakout.
questions.simple: Pass. In a Red market we're mostly cash, because even great setups fail when everything's selling.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65)
fixed before

questions.q: This stock trades through the inside day's high tomorrow morning. How do you get in?
choices: Market order as it goes through
Limit order a cent over the high
Buy premarket on a gap up
questions.answer: Market order as it goes through
questions.why: A market order as it trades through. We market order every entry. When it breaks, you want to be in, not sitting on a limit the stock runs away from. And look at this bar. It's an inside day and a hammer, a long lower wick and a close near the high. That's a good look, even if it's a tad extended from the 50-day. Mark the high the night before and set an alert, so you're ready when it goes. No buys before the open either. The break has to happen in regular hours. A limit under the low just waits for the weakness that kills the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Market order, regular hours, as it goes through.

wrong.Limit order under the low: That waits for the stock to trade under the low, the very thing that cancels the buy.
wrong.Limit order a cent over the high: A limit can sit there unfilled while the stock runs. We use market orders.
wrong.Buy premarket on a gap up: No new buys outside regular hours. Wait for the open.

questions.simple: A market order as it trades over the high, in regular hours. Mark the level and set an alert.

deeper.trap: The careful-looking limit order is the trap. On a real break the price moves fast, and a limit either misses it or fills only on the way back down.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, E58) and a held decision on entry timing
fixed before

questions.story: The last bar is the inside day. Tomorrow you want to buy the break.

questions.q: You're in at 20.71 on the break, stop at 20.47. Where's 3R on this trade?
questions.why: 21.43. Your risk, 1R, is 20.71 minus 20.47, which is 0.24 a share. Three of those is 0.72. Add it to your fill: 20.71 plus 0.72 is 21.43. JBLU got there the next day. 3R is a measuring stick, not an order to sell. We very rarely sell on day 1. Know where it is, then let the trade show you how strong it is.
questions.lesson_line: A small stop makes 3R a small move. Know the number before the open.
questions.simple: Add three times your risk to your fill price. That lands at 21.43.

reasons: a computed key

wrong.$21.19: That's three R added to the stop. Add it to your fill instead.
wrong.$19.99: That's three R under your fill. A long's target sits above it.
wrong.$23.71: That's 3 dollars added, not three R. R is your fill minus your stop.

questions.story: You bought the break the day after the inside day.

questions.q: This one prints an inside day while it's pulling back, and it closes under its 20 EMA. Is this your spot?
choices: No, it's a pause in a range
No, the bar is too narrow
questions.answer: No, it's a pause in a range
questions.why: No. Under the 20 EMA the stock is still leaking. And look further down. It's under a falling 50-day too, sitting right on a flat 200-day. A quiet day down there is a pause in a range, not a spring. We want the inside day at or above a rising line, where buyers have already shown up. So wait for AMZN to get back over the 20 EMA and give you a higher low. That's the spot where I'd want to be involved.
questions.lesson_line: Under the fast line, a quiet day is a stall, not a spring.

wrong.Yes, any inside day works: Buying every inside day is the mistake. Where it sits decides it.
wrong.Yes, buy over its high: Its high still sits in a pullback under the 20 EMA. That's buying a bounce, not a continuation.
wrong.No, the bar is too narrow: Narrow isn't the problem. Where it sits, under the 20 EMA, is.

questions.simple: No. Under the 20 EMA it's just a pause in a range, so wait for it to get back over the line.

reasons: one source: the criteria card, a proposed criterion
fixed before

questions.story: The last bar is an inside day in a pullback, closing under the 20 EMA.

questions.q: You need the 9, 20 and 50 stacked in order before you'll buy an inside day.
questions.why: False. A full stack is nice to see, but it's not a must. The hard line is the 200-day: we don't buy a stock under it. We also want the 50-day riding above the 200-day, with the lines pointed up. That one's mostly a must, not always. Plenty of good inside days come while the 9 is just curling back over the 20.
questions.lesson_line: The stack is a plus. Above the 200-day is the line.
questions.simple: False. The stack is a plus, while the 200-day is the hard line and the 50 over the 200 is mostly a must.

reasons: rests on the hard 200-day rule in the rulebook

questions.q: Fill in the number.
questions.sentence: You bought an inside-day break. If it's still under 1R after ___ trading days, you sell it.
questions.why: 10. A trade that's gone nowhere for two weeks is tying up money a better setup could use. The pause was supposed to release, so a good break should get moving. 1R is what you risked, the distance from your entry to your stop. Slow is fine: VST took 10 days to reach 3R, then ran. Stuck under 1R is different. Sell it and move on.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: 10. A trade still under 1R after two weeks gets sold, so the money can go to a better setup.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C33)

questions.q: Clean inside day at the 20-day, but an unfilled gap down sits 2% overhead. How does that change it?
choices: Lower grade, no room to run
No change, only the bar counts
Better, the gap is a target
questions.answer: Lower grade, no room to run
questions.why: Lower grade. That gap down is where people got trapped. When price comes back up there, a lot of them sell to get out even. So your break runs 2% and hits a wall. I want clear air above the trigger, room to run before anything's in the way. You can still take it. It's just a lower grade, and a lower grade gets a smaller size.
questions.lesson_line: Check the room above before you buy. A gap just overhead is a wall.

wrong.No change, only the bar counts: Room overhead is part of the spot. A gap 2% up is a wall.
wrong.Better, the gap is a target: A gap down overhead is people waiting to get out even. It's a wall, not a magnet.
wrong.It kills the trade outright: It lowers the grade. It doesn't ban the trade.

questions.simple: Lower grade. Sellers trapped in that gap are waiting overhead, so the break has little room.

reasons: one cited fact only (a proposed grade cue)

questions.q: Bulkowski expects an inside day to break out the same way the trend was going in.
questions.why: True. That's Bulkowski's read: expect the break in the direction of the trend going in. It's an expectation, not a promise. He also says no trend is needed before one. That's why we bring the trend ourselves. A leader above its 200-day, trending up, then a quiet day. Now the odds lean our way.
questions.lesson_line: A pause tends to resume the trend. So bring the trend.
questions.simple: True. He expects the break to follow the trend in, which is why we only buy them in uptrends.

reasons: a pattern expectation from the web, not a guarantee

questions.q: Your stop under this inside day's low would sit 6% from the trigger. What's the move?
choices: Pass, wait for a tighter one
Use the mother low, size down
Move the stop to 3%, size down
questions.answer: Pass, wait for a tighter one
questions.why: Pass for now. We like a stop 1 to 3% away, and we'll go up to 5%. This one's 6%, past the line. The fix isn't moving the stop. The low is where the chart says you're wrong, and a stop at 3% just sits in the noise. The mother low at 8% is worse. Wait for a tighter trigger, a day whose low puts your stop inside 5%. I'd rather miss it than take a loss I didn't plan for.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

wrong.Use the mother low, size down: That's 8% away, wider still. Giving it room just means a bigger loss on the same idea.
wrong.Move the stop to 3%, size down: A 3% stop sits above the real low, in the noise. Never move the stop just to fit the size.
wrong.Keep the stop, normal size: Same shares on a 6% stop is a bigger loss than you planned. Past 5% we wait.

questions.story: The inside day is wide: the stop under its low sits 6% from the trigger. The mother bar's low is 8% away.
questions.simple: Pass and wait. The honest stop is past the 5% we'll accept, and moving it puts it in the noise.

deeper.counter: A wide stop isn't a flaw in the stock. It's information. Up to 5% you take it and let the stop set the size. Past that, the better trade is usually the next, tighter trigger.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3, A5) and a stop-size line still held

questions.q: Filled at 41.09 on the break, with the stop at 40.45. How far away is your stop, in percent?
questions.why: 1.56%. 41.09 minus 40.45 is 0.64 a share. 0.64 divided by 41.09, times 100, is 1.56%. That's right in the 1 to 3% we like. This is why we like inside days: a quiet bar gives you a stop close to your buy. ATI's did. One honest flaw on this chart, though. It's well extended from its 50-day. A tight stop keeps the loss small. It doesn't fix a stretched spot. Work it in percent every time. A dollar figure means nothing until you compare it to the price.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stop as a percent of the buy. Quiet bars give small stops.
questions.simple: Your buy minus your stop, divided by the buy, times 100. That comes to 1.56%.

reasons: a computed key

wrong.0.64%: That's the dollar gap read as a percent. Divide it by the buy first.
wrong.15.58%: The decimal slipped one place to the right.
wrong.98.44%: That's the stop divided by the buy, how much of the price is left. Not how far the stop is.

questions.story: You bought the break the day after the inside day.

questions.q: The inside day ran 20.00 to 21.00 and closed at 20.80. Where in its range did it close, 0 at the low and 1 at the high?
questions.why: 0.80, up near the high. Take the close minus the low: 20.80 minus 20.00 is 0.80. Divide by the range, 21.00 minus 20.00, which is 1.00. 0.80 over 1.00 is 0.80. A close up in the top of the range means buyers held it into the bell. I like that picture. It helps the grade, but it's not a rule.
questions.lesson_line: A close near the high means buyers held it. That's the picture I like.
questions.simple: Close minus low, over high minus low. That's 0.80, so it closed near the high.

reasons: a computed key
cue or rule is a held decision
fixed before

wrong.0.99: That's the close divided by the high. Use the range: close minus low, over high minus low.
wrong.1.04: That's the close divided by the low, not by the range.
wrong.1.25: That's flipped: the range over the climb, instead of the climb over the range.

questions.q: Your stock gapped right through your stop this morning. What do you do now?
choices: Hold for the gap to fill
questions.why: Get out. A gap under your stop is the one time the stop gets a second look. The first 30 minutes decide, and that bar's low becomes the new stop. But there's a ceiling. 2R down is 47.40, and 46.70 is under it. The loss is already past 2R, so you're done. Take it and move on. The ceiling is there so one gap can't turn into a disaster.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop gets one look, with a 2R ceiling.

wrong.Hold for the gap to fill: Hoping for the fill is how a small loss gets big.
wrong.Sell half, hold the rest: Past 2R the call is out, not half out.
wrong.Make 46.70 the new stop: That only works while the loss is inside 2R. 46.70 is under 47.40, so you're out.

questions.story: You bought the break at 50.00 with the stop at 48.70. That's 1R of 1.30, so 2R down is 47.40. The next morning it gaps open at 47.80. The first 30-minute bar's low is 46.70.
questions.simple: Get out. The first 30-minute low is past 2R, and 2R is the ceiling.

deeper.counter: The open was already under the stop, so the stop order alone couldn't protect you. Inside 2R, the first 30-minute low becomes the new stop. Past 2R, you're out. It's the one place a stop is allowed to move down, and it has a ceiling.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)
the key is a computed comparison in R

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
choices: Sell a third at the open
Wait for the close to sell
Sell it all at the open
Just raise the stop; no trim
questions.answer: Sell a third at the open
questions.why: Sell a third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, we take that trim at the open. This one opens at 3.5R, past the 3R level, so the first third comes off. The rest stays in with its stop.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through a trim level is the trim. Take it at the open.

wrong.Wait for the close to sell: We take the trim at the open, not later. A stock that opens above a trim level gets that trim at the open.
wrong.Sell it all at the open: The trim is a third at 3R. The rest stays in with its stop.
wrong.Just raise the stop; no trim: Raising the stop is a separate step. A trim level the open has passed is taken at the open.

questions.simple: True. The trend into one is up about half the time, so the bar doesn't pick a direction.

deeper.trap: Don't read 53% as a bullish lean. It's how often the trend in was up, not how often the trade worked.

reasons: a figure on a web page that is updated over time

questions.q: You're up 2R and the stock reports tomorrow after the close. What do you do?
questions.why: Sell before the report. We only hold through earnings when we're up 5R or more. At 2R the report can gap it down past your entry overnight, and no stop catches that. A breakeven stop doesn't help either. The stock can open well under it. If you still like it, you can buy it back after the report, on a new setup.
questions.lesson_line: Hold through a report only at 5R. Below that, be out before it.
questions.story: You're up 2R on an inside-day winner. It reports earnings tomorrow after the close.
choices: Hold, it's working fine so far

wrong.Hold, it's working fine so far: Up 2R isn't enough cushion. A report can take it all back overnight.
wrong.Hold, stop is at breakeven: A gap opens under a breakeven stop just as easily.
wrong.Sell half, hold the rest: Half held through the report is still held through the report. Under 5R, be out.

questions.simple: Sell before the report. We only hold through earnings at 5R or more, because a gap can skip your stop.

deeper.counter: Flip it. The same trade up 5R can be held through the report, because the cushion can absorb a gap. At 2R it can't.

reasons: rests on the rulebook's earnings rule

questions.q: SPY, QQQ and IWM all printed inside days today. Do you trade your inside-day breaks tomorrow?
choices: Wait for the indexes to break
No, sit out the whole week
questions.answer: Wait for the indexes to break
questions.why: Wait for the indexes to pick a side. When the whole market goes quiet at once, the next move can go either way. Quiet comes before a bigger move, up or down. Your breakouts lean on the market. If the indexes break down tomorrow, your breaks fail with them. If they break up, your list goes. So let them show you first. It might cost you a little on the entry. That's cheap.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet indexes break both ways. Let them pick first.

wrong.Yes, inside days point up: An inside day doesn't pick a direction. Quiet comes before a move either way.
wrong.No, sit out the whole week: Wait for the break, not the week. It might come tomorrow.
wrong.Yes, leaders ignore the market: Leaders trade with the market more than people think. Let the indexes go first.

questions.story: SPY, QQQ and IWM, the big index ETFs, all printed inside days today. Your focus list has a few inside-day breaks set for tomorrow.
questions.simple: Wait. A quiet market can break either way, and your breakouts go with it.

reasons: one source: the criteria card, a proposed criterion

questions.q: Crabel took his inside-day profits fast, often at the first day's close. Is that how we exit?
choices: No, we judge the first sell
Yes, at the first profitable close
questions.answer: No, we judge the first sell
questions.why: No. Crabel took profits fast, at the close of the first day or on the first profitable close. We're swing traders. We very rarely sell on day 1, and most of the time we wait until day 3 at the earliest. The first sell is a judgment, often into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Then the rest trails the 9 or 20 EMA. Same bar, a much longer trade.
questions.lesson_line: Same bar, different trade. Ours holds past day 1.

wrong.Yes, same bar, same exit: Same bar, different trade. We hold past day one.
wrong.Yes, at the first profitable close: That's Crabel's other exit. We're not selling that early.
wrong.No, we use Bulkowski's target: His target of twice the pattern height isn't ours either. Ours is a judged first sell and a trail.

questions.simple: No. We rarely sell on day one, and the first sell is a judgment before we trail the rest.

deeper.counter: StockCharts says a narrow-range trade should start working right away. Ours gets more time: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

reasons: rests on the rulebook's trim and trail rules

questions.q: Next morning it opens just over the inside day's high, at 55.02. What's your plan?
choices: Buy 55.02, stop 52.00, and hold it all
Wait for the close, mother-low stop
questions.why: Buy the open at market, 55.02. That's a gap of 0.1% over the trigger, well inside our 4%. Stop a few cents under the inside day's low, at 54.28, which is 1.34% away. The first sell is a judgment: day 3 at the earliest, into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Then trail the rest. NVDA hit 3R in two days. Write it all down before the open, then just execute it.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, first sell, trail. Write it before the open.

wrong.Buy 55.02, stop 52.00, and hold it all: 52.00 isn't where the chart says you're wrong. The stop goes under the inside day's low, 54.28. And you need a sell plan.
wrong.Buy 55.02, stop 54.28, sell half day 1: The stop's right, but we very rarely sell on day 1.
wrong.Wait for the close, mother-low stop: We buy as it trades through the trigger, never at the close. And the mother low is the wide-stop mistake.

questions.story: An inside day four days after a breakout, on light volume. Tomorrow it opens a hair over the high, at 55.02.
questions.simple: Buy at market, stop just under the inside day's low, no first sell before day 3, then trail the rest.

deeper.example: Walk it in R. One R is the fill minus the stop. R is the measuring stick, not the sell signal. The plan is written before the open, so there's nothing to argue about when it moves.

reasons: entry timing is a held decision (D-003)
fixed before

questions.q: Our market filter reads Yellow and you have two good inside days lined up. How do you play it?
choices: Only if one is an A+
Mostly cash, no buys at all
questions.why: Take them, smaller and fewer. The reading tells you how hard to press. Green is full risk for the grade and up to 10 positions. In Yellow you dial it back: less risk per trade and fewer names. Orange is A+ only, and Red is mostly cash. Yellow means the market's mixed. Good setups still work, they just fail more often, so you don't want a full book of them.
questions.lesson_line: Yellow is still a go. Smaller and fewer.

wrong.Same as Green, full risk: Full risk is Green. Yellow means you dial it back.
wrong.Mostly cash, no buys at all: That's Red, and even Red is a guide. Yellow still trades.

questions.story: The market filter in our app reads Yellow. Two good inside days sit on your list for tomorrow.
questions.simple: Take them, but smaller and fewer than in Green, because a mixed market fails more breakouts.

deeper.trap: The reading is a guide to how much you trade, not a pass on the setup. Each one still has to be a leader, above the 200-day, with a stop that fits.

reasons: rests on the rulebook's market reading, a guide that may change

questions.q: Stopped out Monday. Wednesday prints a new inside day and Thursday trades over its high. Back in?
choices: Yes, double size to win it back
questions.why: Yes, as a brand new trade. A stop-out isn't a verdict on the stock. If the setup triggers again, you take it with its own stop, a few cents under Wednesday's inside low, and your normal size. This is your second try this week. We allow up to 3 in a week and 6 in a month on one stock. Past that, the stock is telling you something.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out isn't a verdict. The next trigger is a new trade.

wrong.No, one try per week: The limit is 3 tries a week and 6 a month. This is try two.
wrong.Yes, stop under Monday's low: Monday's low belongs to the old trade. The new stop goes under Wednesday's inside day.
wrong.Yes, double size to win it back: Sizing up to win it back is how one loss turns into two big ones. Same risk, same rules.

questions.story: You bought an inside-day break on Monday, your first try on this stock this week, and got stopped out. Wednesday prints a new inside day and Thursday trades over its high.
questions.simple: Yes. A new trigger is a new trade, with its own stop and normal size.

deeper.trap: The pull after a loss is to size up and win it back. A re-entry is a new trade with every rule, and it still counts toward the tries.

reasons: rests on the rulebook's re-entry and tries rules

questions.q: Your leader broke out of its base Friday, and you missed it. What do you watch for next?
choices: An inside day or two up here
questions.answer: An inside day or two up here
questions.why: An inside day or two up here. After a breakout a leader often rests a day or two near the highs. That quiet bar gives you a second way in, with a level to buy and a stop close by. It's the same note from the Sunday Scans on SHOP: if not in, look for an inside day or two up here. Chasing 6% up has no stop that makes sense. We never buy more than 4% over the buy point.
questions.lesson_line: Missed the breakout. Watch for the quiet day after it.

wrong.A deep pullback to the 200-day: A leader that just broke out may never get back there. Watch for a pause near the highs.
wrong.Buy Monday, even 6% up: We never buy more than 4% over the buy point. Wait for the quiet day.
wrong.An NR7, the narrowest day: A narrow day can still poke over yesterday's high. You want an inside day, both ends inside.

questions.story: A leader breaks out of a base on Friday. You're not in.
questions.simple: Watch for an inside day or two near the highs. It gives you a level to buy and a close stop.

deeper.example: From the Sunday Scans on SHOP: it finally broke out on Friday. If you weren't in, look for an inside day or two up here.

reasons: rests on the owner's published Sunday Scan words

questions.q: Two leaders, two inside days, two different spots. Which one do you want?
questions.answer: A, room above and a good market
questions.why: A. Both are leaders above the 200-day, and both bars look the same. The spot is what's different. A is just after a breakout, with clear air above and a Green market behind it. B has an old high right overhead, where trapped buyers want out. And the indexes are quiet, so the market hasn't picked a side. Same bar, very different odds. I'd take A and let B wait.
questions.lesson_line: Same bar, different spot. The spot decides.
questions.story: Two inside days on different days, both leaders above the 200-day. A: just after a breakout, Green market, clear air overhead. B: under an old high just overhead, with the indexes printing inside days.
choices: A, room above and a good market
B, the old high is a target
Same, the bar is the same

wrong.B, the old high is a target: An old high overhead is supply. It's a wall, not a magnet.
wrong.B, the indexes are coiling: Quiet indexes can break either way. That's a reason to wait, not to buy.
wrong.Same, the bar is the same: The bar's the same. The room and the market aren't, and they carry the edge.

questions.simple: A. It has room to run and a market behind it, while B has a wall overhead.

deeper.trap: The trap is grading the bar. Both are inside days above the 200-day, so the bar doesn't separate them. Look at the room overhead and the market behind it.

reasons: the A+ and B- location rows are a held decision (D-066)
fixed before

questions.q: A few days after a breakout, this leader prints an inside day. Check the 50-day and 200-day. Do you take it?
choices: Yes, a tad extended, but stop is tight
Pass, too far over the 50-day to buy
Yes, a tiny bar is always better
questions.answer: Yes, a tad extended, but stop is tight
questions.why: Yes, but be honest about it. Price is over a rising 50-day and 200-day, and the 50 is over the 200. The lines are right. It's also a tad extended. It sits well over the 50-day, and the 200 is way down there. Here's why I still take it. The inside day came four days after the breakout, on light volume. That's a leader resting, not tiring. And the quiet bar puts the stop close: 54.28 under a 55.02 buy, 1.34%. Wrong, and it's a small loss. The next session opened just over the high, and NVDA hit 3R in two days.
questions.lesson_line: Lines and location first, then the bar.

wrong.Pass, too far over the 50-day to buy: It is a tad extended. But it's four days past a breakout, and the inside day gives you a stop about 1.34% away. That risk is worth taking.
wrong.Yes, a tiny bar is always better: Tiny isn't the reason. It's where it sits, and the tight stop it gives you.

questions.simple: Yes. It's a tad extended, but it's resting days after a breakout, and the stop is tight.

deeper.trap: Do the lines first, then the bar. An inside day under the 200-day isn't ours, however clean it looks. A full stack of the fast lines is only a plus.

reasons: rests on the hard 200-day rule
the chart read rests on the dossier

questions.q: The last bar looks tight after a breakout. Is it an inside day you can buy over the high?
choices: No, its high is over yesterday's
Yes, narrowest day in a week
Yes, its low is inside yesterday's
No, it's too narrow to trade
questions.answer: No, its high is over yesterday's
questions.why: No. Its high is 0.30% over yesterday's high, even though the low sits 1.26% inside. Both ends have to be inside. This MSFT bar is a narrow-range day after a breakout, a different animal. Bought over its high it went 1.7R, but that says nothing about the rule. Check both ends before you call it.
questions.lesson_line: Narrow isn't inside. Check the high.

wrong.Yes, narrowest day in a week: A narrow day can still poke over yesterday's high. This one did.
wrong.Yes, its low is inside yesterday's: One end inside is half the definition. The high is over yesterday's.
wrong.No, it's too narrow to trade: Narrow isn't banned. It fails because its high is over yesterday's.

questions.simple: No. The high pokes over yesterday's high, so only one end is inside.

deeper.trap: Hindsight trap: one good result can't turn a narrow-range day into an inside day.

reasons: bar numbers read from our own bars
tied to the held decision D-002 on the narrow-range look-alike

questions.q: Leader at a rising 20-day, Green market, a 1.5% stop. At 10:20 the high trades. Your call?
choices: Pass, the bar alone is random
Buy it, stop at the mother low
Buy it, but at half size
questions.why: Buy it, at market as the high trades. On its own the bar is close to random. Here it isn't on its own. A leader above the 200-day with the 50 over it, an inside day at a rising 20-day, a Green market, no earnings for weeks. The stop goes a few cents under the inside low, 1.5% away, right in our 1 to 3%. That's the picture from the Sunday Scans: an inside day and a higher low at a rising 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: When the stock, the spot and the market all say yes, the quiet day is the door.

wrong.Pass, the bar alone is random: Alone, yes. Here the stock, the spot and the market all agree.
wrong.Buy it, stop at the mother low: The stop goes under the inside day's low. The mother low is the wide-stop mistake.
wrong.Buy it, but at half size: Green market and everything lines up. Nothing here calls for half.

questions.story: A clean inside day at a rising 20-day in a leader above its 200-day, its 50-day above the 200. Green market, no earnings for weeks, the stop 1.5% under the trigger. The next day at 10:20, the high trades.
questions.simple: Buy it. The stock, the spot and the market all agree, and the stop is tight.

deeper.trap: Don't read 'close to random' as 'never'. In our test only 26.7% reached 3R and 88.2% were eventually stopped. We buy it where the stock, the spot and the market agree, then manage it with the stop, the sells and the trail.

reasons: entry timing is a held decision (D-003)
fixed before

questions.q: For an inside-day buy, a mental stop is fine as long as you're watching the screen.
questions.why: False. Every position gets a real stop order with your broker. A stop in your head is a hope. You look away, the market drops, and you freeze. Put the order a few cents under the inside day's low the moment you're filled. It still can't catch a gap. If it opens under your stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop, and past 2R you're out.
questions.lesson_line: A stop in your head isn't a stop.
questions.simple: False. Put a real stop order with your broker, because a stop in your head fails right when you need it.

deeper.trap: A real stop order is not the whole answer. When a stock gaps open under the stop, our gap rule applies. The first 30-minute low becomes the new stop, and a loss past 2R means out.

reasons: rests on the rulebook's real-stop-order rule

questions.q: You've graded an inside-day setup a B-. It's still a trade. How big do you go?
choices: Skip it, A and B only
questions.why: Smaller than normal. The grade sets the size. A and B setups get normal size, A+ gets sized up, and B- or lower gets sized down. A B- means something's off, maybe the spot or the room overhead. It can still work. But the odds are worse, so you put less on it. How you grade is your judgment. Once you've graded it, the size follows.
questions.lesson_line: The grade sets the size. A+ up, A and B normal, B- down.

wrong.Bigger, like an A+: Sizing up is for A+. A B- gets less, not more.
wrong.Normal, same as a B: Normal size is for A and B. B- or lower gets sized down.
wrong.Skip it, A and B only: A B- is still a trade, just a smaller one.

questions.simple: Smaller than normal. A weaker setup gets less money, so a loss there costs less.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook, D38 and E50

questions.q: Look at the last three bars on this chart. What have you got?
questions.story: Judge the last three bars after the last close.
questions.why: A double inside day. The first of the three bars is the mother bar. The middle one sits inside it, and the last one sits inside the middle. That's two inside days in a row, each inside the day before. TSLA is winding tighter and nobody's picked a side yet. It's still only a way in. It matters when a bigger setup sits behind it.
questions.lesson_line: Count from the mother bar. Each one has to fit inside the day before.
questions.simple: A double. The middle bar sits inside the first, and the last sits inside the middle.

wrong.A triple inside day: The first bar is the mother bar, so it doesn't count. That's two inside days.
wrong.A single inside day: The last bar sits inside the middle one, so it counts too.
wrong.No inside day at all: Both ends of the last bar sit inside the middle bar. That's an inside day.

deeper.counter: Mish calls two inside days in a row an even clearer sign of indecision.
